kale.name: Kale
kale.desc: Kale, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
kale.offers: Kale is a sturdy leafy green that is a good source of vitamin C and vitamin A, with plenty of vitamin K and fibre.
kale.how: Simmer it in soups and stews, sauté with garlic, or massage raw leaves with a little oil and lemon for a salad. Stems are tougher: slice them thinly or cook them longer.
kale.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for kale.
kale.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS). No cycle-specific claim is made.

sweet-potato.name: Sweet potato
sweet-potato.desc: Sweet potato, cooked, baked in skin, flesh, without salt
sweet-potato.state: baked in skin, flesh only, no salt
sweet-potato.portion: ½ cup mashed or cubed, baked flesh (USDA: 1 cup = 200 g)
sweet-potato.offers: Sweet potato is a soft, naturally sweet root that is an excellent source of vitamin A (as beta-carotene) and gives potassium, vitamin C and fibre.
sweet-potato.how: Bake whole until soft, then eat with the skin or mash the flesh; roast in wedges; or add cubes to curries and soups.
sweet-potato.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for sweet potato.
sweet-potato.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS). No cycle-specific claim is made.

beets.name: Beets
beets.portion: ½ cup sliced, cooked (USDA: 0.5 cup = 85 g)
beets.offers: Beets are a sweet, earthy root vegetable with folate and potassium.
beets.how: Roast or boil until tender, then slice into salads, blend into soups or dips, or grate raw into slaws.
beets.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for beets.
beets.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS). No cycle-specific claim is made.

carrot.name: Carrot
carrot.offers: Carrots are a crunchy, sweet root vegetable and a rich source of vitamin A (from beta-carotene), with some potassium and fibre.
carrot.how: Eat raw as sticks or grated, roast with olive oil, or simmer into soups and stews. Cooking with a little fat helps your body absorb the beta-carotene.
carrot.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for carrot.
carrot.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS). No cycle-specific claim is made.

chickpea.name: Chickpea
chickpea.desc: Chickpeas (garbanzo beans, bengal gram), mature seeds, cooked, boiled, without salt
chickpea.offers: Chickpeas are a filling pulse with plant protein, fibre, folate, iron and zinc.
chickpea.how: Add to soups, curries and salads, roast until crisp, or blend into hummus. Serve with a vitamin C food such as peppers or lemon: it helps your body absorb plant iron.
chickpea.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for chickpea.
chickpea.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS). No cycle-specific claim is made.

quinoa.name: Quinoa
quinoa.offers: Quinoa is a seed cooked like a grain. It gives plant protein, magnesium, folate, iron and zinc, and it is naturally gluten free.
quinoa.how: Rinse, then simmer in about twice its volume of water until the little rings appear. Use as a base for bowls, stir into soups, or serve warm with vegetables.
quinoa.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for quinoa.
quinoa.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS). No cycle-specific claim is made.

almond.name: Almond
almond.portion: 30 g (USDA reference amount), a small handful
almond.offers: Almonds are a crunchy tree nut with plant protein, fibre, magnesium, iron and zinc. They are energy dense, so a small handful goes a long way.
almond.how: Eat as a snack, chop over porridge or salads, or blend into nut butter. Soak and peel for a milder taste in sauces.
almond.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for almond.
almond.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS). No cycle-specific claim is made.

flaxseeds.name: Flaxseeds
flaxseeds.offers: Flaxseeds are tiny seeds rich in fibre and fats, with magnesium, iron and zinc. They are eaten in small amounts, which is why the serving is a spoonful.
flaxseeds.how: Grind just before use (whole seeds often pass through undigested), then stir into porridge, yoghurt or smoothies, or mix into batters and bread. Keep ground seed in the fridge.
flaxseeds.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for flaxseeds.
flaxseeds.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS). No cycle-specific claim is made.

blueberry.name: Blueberry
blueberry.portion: 140 g (USDA reference amount), about a generous handful
blueberry.offers: Blueberries are small, sweet berries with vitamin C and a little potassium. They are low in fat and easy to eat as they are.
blueberry.how: Eat fresh, stir into yoghurt or porridge, blend into smoothies, or bake into muffins and pancakes. Frozen berries work well in cooking and smoothies.
blueberry.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for blueberry.
blueberry.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS). No cycle-specific claim is made.

tomato.name: Tomato
tomato.desc: Tomatoes, red, ripe, raw, year round average
tomato.offers: Tomatoes are juicy, low-energy fruits eaten as vegetables, with vitamin C and potassium.
tomato.how: Slice into salads and sandwiches, roast until sweet, simmer into sauces and soups, or eat cherry tomatoes whole. A drizzle of olive oil suits them.
tomato.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for tomato.
tomato.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS). No cycle-specific claim is made.

oat.name: Oat
oat.desc: Oats, whole grain, rolled, old fashioned
oat.portion: 40 g dry rolled oats (USDA reference amount) before cooking
oat.offers: Rolled oats are a whole grain with fibre (including beta-glucan), plant protein, magnesium, iron and zinc. Amounts here are for the dry oats, before cooking.
oat.how: Simmer into porridge with milk or water, soak overnight, or add to baking, pancakes and granola. Top with fruit and nuts or seeds.
oat.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for oat.
oat.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS). No cycle-specific claim is made.

chia-seeds.name: Chia seeds
chia-seeds.portion: 1 ounce (28 g) of seeds (USDA: 1 oz = 28.35 g), about two tablespoons
chia-seeds.offers: Chia seeds are tiny seeds that swell and turn gel-like in liquid. They are very high in fibre and give magnesium, iron and zinc.
chia-seeds.how: Stir into yoghurt, porridge or smoothies, or soak in milk for a pudding. Because they absorb liquid, soak them first rather than eating a spoonful dry, and drink water with them.
chia-seeds.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for chia seeds.
chia-seeds.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS). No cycle-specific claim is made.
